newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Bears bludgeon Australian dlr to 2-yr closing low.
newsitem.headline: Bears bludgeon Australian dlr to 2-yr closing low.

text.p: The Australian dollar slumped to its lowest local close in two years Wednesday as dealers found new reasons to be bearish at every turn.

They said U.S. and Swiss banks led a sustained assault all morning, dumping at least A$400-A$500 million and driving the currency to a hair-raising brush with critical support around US$0.7510. Exporter and options-related bids held there, but only managed to squeeze a 20-pip bounce out of a short market.
"The Aussie's actually hung on well considering the scale of the selling," said Steve Shuster, head of forex at Citibank.
"But you have to expect offshore guys to test US$0.7300/10 again to see exactly what bids are there," he added. "That will decide if we wake up tomorrow to US$0.7280 or US$0.7380."
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar had been flattened to US$0.7325/30, its lowest domestic finish since July 19 1995, from an early US$0.7345/50 and US$0.7360/65 late here Tuesday.

Bulls did manage to stave off a break of the 1996 intra-day low at US$0.7305, which would have been a final nail in the chart coffin and set the scene for a fall to US$0.7070. Traders said the market was very short and the currency oversold after falling steadily for four months, so a bounce was long overdue.
A reasonable target for such a rally would normally be the US$0.7430/80 area, but most felt the market was too bearish, and the risk of another rate cut too great, to sustain that.
"Nobody wants to chase it higher because they fear, quite rightly, that a firmer dollar would simply give the RBA more room to cut rates again," said one dealer.

He added the market was still smarting from the last easing in May which caught many by surprise. That saw money rates sink below those in the U.S. -- a situation without precedent and one not to the taste of offshore investors used to thinking of the A$ as a high yielder -- as the market feared further cuts ahead.
Most analysts think the RBA will indeed cut again, possibly after consumer price and wages data next week which are expected to confirm the extremely favourable outlook for inflation.

Today's figures on consumer confidence showed a 1.1 percent rise in July suggesting all the media talk of further rate cuts was filtering through. However, the gain only partially recouped losses of 5.8 percent in the previous three months.

The threat of another easing was cited by Goldman Sachs as a reason to sell the dollar in its latest weekly currency report. The U.S. investment bank had a three-month target of 73 cents but said a fall below 70 cents could not be ruled out.
Traders said the warning was no surprise since Goldman, along with a who's who of other investment houses, had been a persistent seller of the currency in recent weeks.

The Goldman report was equally downbeat on the New Zealand dollar saying the Kiwi would not be fair value until it hit 60 U.S. cents. The Kiwi was down sharply at US$0.6590/03 from US$0.6648/58 late Tuesday. The A$ had the better of the exchange here and edged higher to NZ$1.1134/50 from NZ$1.1056/72.
The local dollar was also troubled by talk U.K. company ICI was repatriating funds from the sale of its 62.4 percent holding in ICI Australia, the term sof which were finalised last week.
The sale of the shares was estimated to have netted the British company around A$2.2 billion.

Commodity prices had been another negative recently with the influential Commodity Research Bureau index plumbing two year lows at 232.01 last week. It had steadied somewhat since with a bounce to 235.15, but remained short of former pivotal support at 236.00 and some key Australian commodities like gold, copper and wheat remained in downtrends.
On the crosses the A$ found some support from a firmer US$/yen and rose to 84.95/05 yen from 84.00/10, which in turn helped it edge to 56.6 on its trade weighted index from 56.5.
